lead: Today's readings set side by side the darkness that follows when God is pushed aside and the light that shines when he is met. Paul describes a humanity that “exchanged the truth about God for a lie” and was handed over to its own desires. At Bethany, near the tomb of Lazarus, Martha meets Jesus and hears, “I am the resurrection and the life.” Paul's picture of death is answered by Christ's word of life. The key words are exchange and believe.

r.h: They exchanged the truth about God for a lie
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57–58, to a church he had not yet visited. After stating his theme, that the Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith (1:16–17), he shows that all, Gentiles and Jews alike, need that salvation (1:18–3:20). He begins with the pagan world: God can be known through the things he has made (1:20), but people did not honour him as God (1:21) and exchanged his glory for images (1:23). Today's verses describe what follows.

The thought has a Jewish background, above all Wisdom 13–14, which says that the worship of idols is “the beginning and cause and end of every evil” (Wisdom 14:27). Then, in 2:1, Paul turns on the reader who has been nodding in agreement: “you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you judge others.”
str: vv. 24–25: God gave them up to impurity, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie.
vv. 26–27: God gave them up to degrading passions.
v. 28: God gave them up to a debased mind.
vv. 29–31: a long list of vices.
v. 32: knowing God's decree, they not only do these things but applaud others who do them.
kw: Three times (vv. 24, 26, 28). God does not push anyone into sin; he lets people have what they have chosen, and the choice becomes its own punishment. It is the same verb Paul uses of Christ, “handed over to death for our trespasses” (4:25), and of the Father who “gave him up for all of us” (8:32).

The key word of the passage: God's glory exchanged for images (v. 23, a related verb), the truth for a lie (v. 25), the natural for the unnatural (v. 26). Sin is shown as a bad bargain, a trading of the real for the false.
Against the order the Creator has placed in things. Paul's argument rests on Genesis 1: those who refuse to honour the Creator end by losing sight of the order of his creation.
vv: because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
In the middle of the darkest passage Paul breaks into a blessing. A devout Jew could hardly name the Creator without blessing him.
And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind

There is a play on words in the Greek: they did not think it fit (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, so he gave them up to an unfit (adokimon) mind. When God is refused, even the power to judge rightly is damaged.
They know God’s decree, that those who practice such things deserve to die
The last stage is not weakness but approval: to call evil good. Isaiah had warned: “Ah, you who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20).
ch: The Church reads these verses as Paul meant them: as the first step of an argument that ends in mercy. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; they are now justified by his grace as a gift” (3:23–24). No reader stands outside the list of verses 29–31, which includes envy, gossip and boasting. From verses 26–27 the Church draws her teaching that homosexual acts are contrary to the natural law; in the same place she teaches that persons with such tendencies must be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and that every sign of unjust discrimination must be avoided (CCC 2357–2358). All are called to chastity, and all are offered the same mercy.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, has died. When Jesus heard of his illness he stayed two days longer where he was (11:6), saying that the illness was “for God’s glory” (11:4). Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometres from Jerusalem. The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest of the signs in John's Gospel, and it leads directly to the decision to put Jesus to death (11:53).

Many had come to console the sisters, as Jewish custom asked of friends during the days of mourning. A later rabbinic tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; whether or not that belief lies behind the “four days” here, John means that Lazarus is beyond all doubt dead.
str: vv. 17–19: Jesus arrives; Lazarus four days in the tomb; many come to console.
vv. 20–22: Martha goes out to meet him: sorrow and trust.
vv. 23–24: “Your brother will rise again”; Martha's faith in the last day.
vv. 25–26: “I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?”
kw: Martha uses the word of the general resurrection at the end of time, which many Jews of her day believed (Daniel 12:2; compare Acts 23:8). Jesus tells her that the resurrection is not only an event in the future: it is a person, standing before her.

One of the great “I am” sayings of John's Gospel: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the way, the truth and the life. They echo the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
The question is put to Martha, and through her to every reader. John says he wrote his Gospel “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God” (20:31).
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
Grief speaks honestly to Jesus. Mary will say the same words (11:32). Jesus does not rebuke the complaint.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,
Bodily death remains, but it no longer has the last word. The life Jesus gives begins now, in faith and Baptism, and death does not break it.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.
Martha's confession is as full as Peter's in Matthew 16:16, and it uses the very titles of John's statement of purpose (20:31). She makes it before she has seen her brother raised.
ch: The Church hears in this Gospel her faith in the resurrection of the body: Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, saw in Lazarus four days dead an image of the soul long bound by the habit of sin, whom the voice of Christ still calls out of the tomb (Tractates on John 49, in substance). Martha, often remembered only for being busy (Luke 10:40), is here the one who makes the great confession of faith.

qa: Why did Jesus wait two days before going to Bethany?

John gives the reason in Jesus' own words: the illness was “for God’s glory, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (11:4). He also says plainly that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus (11:5). The delay was not indifference; it made room for a greater sign, through which many came to believe (11:45). God's delays in our own lives can also hide a larger mercy.
study: Paul says that sin begins with exchanging the truth about God for a lie. What false “gods” compete for the first place in my life?
Jesus asks Martha, “Do you believe this?” How would I answer him at the grave of someone I love?
